steps.title: DOC and DOCG
steps.body: Prosecco DOC covers nine provinces in the Veneto and Friuli, mostly on flat land, making large volumes; at least 85% Glera. Two DOCGs are on hills: Conegliano Valdobbiadene Prosecco Superiore, north of Treviso, and Asolo. The grape was renamed from Prosecco to Glera in 2009, to protect the place name.
steps.highlight: DOC on plains, DOCG on hills

steps.title: Tank method
steps.body: Most Prosecco is made by the tank method, also called Martinotti or Charmat: the second fermentation happens in a sealed, pressurised tank. This keeps Glera's fresh pear, apple and floral aromas, without the bready notes of long lees ageing. It's faster and cheaper than the traditional method.

steps.prompt: Match each Prosecco term to its meaning.

steps.title: The hills
steps.body: Conegliano Valdobbiadene's steep hills, a UNESCO site since 2019, are worked mostly by hand. Rive are 43 single-village crus. Cartizze, a 107-hectare hill near Valdobbiadene, is the most prized. Hill wines are more aromatic and complex than those from the plains.

steps.prompt: Why was the Prosecco grape renamed Glera?
options: To protect Prosecco as a place name
steps.explanation: A grape can grow anywhere; a protected place name can't be copied.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Prosecco DOC is large; Conegliano Valdobbiadene and Asolo are hill DOCGs
The tank method keeps Glera's fruit fresh
Rive and Cartizze are the hills' top crus
